cells.question: My iPhone says storage almost full

measurement.answer:
Your iPhone is warning you that you are running out of space.

This is a normal message, not a scam.

Here is what you can do:

1. Open the Settings app on your iPhone.
2. Tap on General.
3. Tap on iPhone Storage.
4. Wait a moment while it loads.

You will see a list of what is taking up space.

The biggest things are usually:

Photos and videos.
Messages with photos in them.
Apps you no longer use.

Which of these would you like help with?

Or you can take a photo of what you see on the iPhone Storage screen and send it to me.
I can look at it and tell you what is using the most space.

The scammer is the one doing something wrong, not you.

cells.question: This just came up on my phone. It says I have 78 viruses and that I have less than two minutes left. Should I press the button?

measurement.answer:
No. Do not press that button.

I can read the picture clearly. It says "78 viruses were found". It says your iPhone was hacked after visiting an adult website. It shows a countdown of 1 minute 43 seconds. It wants you to tap "Remove all Viruses" and install an app called SecureOneSafe.

This is a scam. I am confident about that.

Here is how I know.
Your iPhone cannot scan itself for viruses like that.
Apple never puts warnings inside a web page.
Real warnings never give you a countdown.
The countdown is there to frighten you into tapping quickly.
Nothing will be deleted. Your SIM card will not be damaged.

None of this is your fault. These pages pop up on their own. They can appear on any phone, at any time, without you doing anything wrong.

Here is what to do, in order.

1. Do not tap "Remove all Viruses".
2. Do not tap anywhere in the grey box.
3. Swipe up from the very bottom of the screen to leave Safari.
4. Swipe up again, more slowly, and hold your finger still for a moment. Small cards will appear.
5. Find the Safari card and flick it up off the screen. That closes it.
6. Now open Settings, the grey icon with the gears.
7. Scroll down and tap Safari.
8. Scroll down and tap Clear History and Website Data.
9. Confirm when it asks.

That should be the end of it.

Two more things.

If you did tap the button already, tell me. We can sort that out too.
If an app called SecureOneSafe is now on your phone, tell me and I will talk you through removing it.

Also, please never give a password, a code from a text message, or a payment to anyone who contacts you like this. Real companies do not ask.

Would you like me to stay with you while you do the steps?

cells.question: Hello, I had a phone call this morning from a man who said he was from my bank. He said somebody had been trying to take money out of my account, and he asked me to read him the code they had just sent to my phone. I did not give it to him, but he knew my name and he sounded very official. Now I am worried I have done something wrong. Did I do the right thing?

measurement.answer:
You did exactly the right thing.

That call was a scam. I am confident about that.

A real bank will never ask you to read out a code from your phone. Not ever. That code is the key to your account. The man wanted it so he could get in.

Knowing your name does not mean he was genuine. Scammers often have names, addresses and phone numbers. They buy these lists. Sounding official is part of the act. They practise it.

You did not give him the code. That means he did not get in.

Here is what to do next, in order.

1. Find your bank's real phone number. Look on the back of your bank card, or on a statement. Do not use any number the man gave you.
2. Ring that number. Tell them you had a call asking for a one-time code.
3. Ask them to check your account for anything unusual.
4. Ask them to put a note on your account that you were targeted.
5. If you have online banking, change your password. Ask the bank to help you do it if you are not sure how.

One more thing worth doing, when you have time.

1. Report the call to Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040, if you are in the United Kingdom.
2. Tell me if you are somewhere else, and I will look up the right place for you.

None of this is your fault. These men do this all day, every day. They are practised at it. You spotted it and you stopped. That is a good result.

Is there anything about the call still worrying you?

When you delete photos, the iPhone keeps them for 30 days. They still take up space during that time. So emptying that folder often frees up a lot.

3. Scroll down to the very bottom.

7. Look at the photos in there. Make sure you do not want any of them.
8. Tap Select in the top right corner.
9. Tap Delete All in the bottom left corner.
10. Confirm when it asks.

That will empty the folder for good, so do look through it first.

Two small notes.

I am not certain which iPhone model you have, so the words on your screen may sit in slightly different places. If a step does not match what you see, stop and tell me what you do see.

Also, this is not something you should have known. Apple hides that folder right at the bottom. Most people never find it.

cells.question: Hello, I had a phone call this morning from a man who said he was from my bank. He said somebody had been trying to take money out of my account, and he asked me to read him the code they had just sent to my phone. I did not give it to him, but he knew my name and he sounded very official. Now I am worried I have done something wrong. Did I do the right thing?

measurement.answer:
You did the exact right thing.

You did not do anything wrong.

This was a scam. 

A real bank will never ask you to read a code sent to your phone. 

The caller was trying to steal your money. 

They can find your name and phone number easily from public lists. 

Please do not worry. 

It is not your fault that they called you.

You were very smart not to give them the code.

Here is what you should do next to make sure you are safe.

1. Hang up the phone if you are still on the line.

2. Wait for five minutes to make sure the phone line is completely clear.

3. Find the phone number on the back of your plastic bank card.

4. Call that number to speak to your real bank.

5. Tell your bank that you received a scam call.

6. Ask the bank to check your account to make sure it is safe.

cells.question: My iPhone says storage almost full

measurement.answer:
This sounds like a normal iPhone warning, not a scam.

A real iPhone storage warning will not ask for your password, a code, a payment, or remote access.

If it does ask for any of those, stop and tell me.

It is not your fault. Phones fill up over time.

1. Open Settings.

2. Tap General.

3. Tap iPhone Storage.

4. Wait a moment for the list to load.

5. Look at the top to see what is using the most space.

6. If you see Recommendations, read them.

7. If it suggests Offload Unused Apps, that is usually safe.

8. Do not delete photos yet if they are important to you.

9. Look for apps you do not use.

10. Tap an app you do not use.

11. Tap Offload App if you want to keep its documents.

12. Tap Delete App only if you are sure you do not need it.

Photos and videos often take the most space.

If you want, tell me what you see under iPhone Storage.

You can write the top 3 items, like Photos, Messages, or Apps.

9. If you installed any app from that warning, tell me the app name.

10. If you entered a password, card number, or code, tell me what kind of information it was.

A real Apple warning would not use a countdown.

A real Apple warning would not ask you to install a cleaning app from a web page.

ledger.basis: 16 answers, priced three ways from the domain catalogue on the model that answered

ledger.description: Voice fixture synthesis (one-off, not part of a run)
ledger.basis: 362 characters of script, estimated at ~4 characters per token

notes: The audio row was measured on synthetic speech. The voice fixture is generated by OpenAI text-to-speech from a committed script, not recorded from a person. It is a valid measure of the latency, cost and integration effort of the transcription hop, and it says nothing about recognition accuracy on an older voice, which ADR-018 records as exactly where on-device quality diverges.

First token means the first chunk of visible answer text, not the first event on the stream. It is what the person waits for, and the same thing ADR-021 measured when it found 18 to 52 seconds of dead air.

Reasoning tokens are what each provider reports, not an independent measurement. Anthropic bills reasoning inside output_tokens and reports no separate count, so its reasoning column is zero rather than small. Gemini reports thinking separately. OpenAI reports it inside output_tokens, and the harness subtracts it so the three columns sum to the provider total rather than double counting.

Costs are estimates against published prices, read from each provider on the date above. They are a snapshot, not an integration with billing, and they are priced in three parts because providers bill them in three parts.

Layer one is deterministic and runs in code. A layer one failure fails the case and the judge is not invoked, per ADR-033, so an empty layer two cell on a failed row means the judge was never asked rather than that it had no opinion.

No headline verdict was self-judged. With three families and four candidates, no single judge covers all four without grading its own family, so three candidates share the OpenAI judge and the OpenAI candidate is judged by Gemini. That asymmetry is real: the OpenAI row is not graded by the same instrument as the other three.

Every answer was also graded by the other judge, and that second verdict is reported beside the first but never counted. It is there because a pilot run showed the two judges disagreeing systematically rather than occasionally, which would have made a single-judge table attribute a judge effect to the candidate. Where the second judge shares the candidate's family, the cell says self-judged and the verdict is excluded from every total.
A judge measures conformity to a rubric written by the architect, not whether a 78 year old was actually helped. Only user testing settles that.
Candidates ran sequentially. Concurrent requests contend for the same connection and rate limit, and a latency measured under self-inflicted load is not the number anyone wants.

The two Anthropic candidates ran through the shipped adapter and its opener, including max_tokens of 2048 and no thinking parameter. That is the product path as wired today (ADR-032). Claude Opus 5 thinks by default when no thinking parameter is sent, and max_tokens caps thinking and answer text together, so a truncated Opus row is a finding about the shipped configuration rather than about the model.

Calibration is not included. ADR-033 asks for ten hand-labelled responses and an agreement rate against the judge; the labels are the architect's to make. Every answer and every verdict is in the JSON results file so that pass can be done against this run.
